                         BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

                                           SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349

   APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION
SERVICES CORPORATION FOR A CERTIFICATE OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL
             COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL 765-kV TRANSMISSION LINE

                                          JOHN BURROW'S INITIAL BRIEF


   John Burrow ("Mr. Burrow") timely files this Initial Briefto the State Office ofAdministrative Hearings ("SOAH")
    Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs") regarding Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC's ("Oncor's") and LCRA
Transmission Services Corporation's ("LCRA's")(collectively, "Applicants"') application for a certificate of convenience
                   and necessity ("CCN") for Bell County East to Bill Hill 765-kV transmission line.

     Mr. Burrow respectfully requests the SOAH ALJs and the Commission to properly and rightfully determine this
         application does not meet PURA requirements and to therefore find the application must be DENIED.

I. INTRODUCTION

I, John M. Burrow, Pro Se Intervenor, Party Number 811, Private Landowner, Route Links G71, G72, and G73, ground
zero in Bell County Texas, am writing this post hearing initial brief without the benefit of having the certified hearing on
merit transcripts. One can say "I'm just winging it" I am one of 1,400 landowners that were notified of the subject
application after March 26,2026. We did not have the opportunity to participate and provide meaningful comment in a
public meeting forum. Over the last two months, I have been forced to navigate in a legal environment with no
experience or legal representation, so I ask the SOAH ALJ's for legal leniency if I am not following format, standards,
protocol, or criteria. My intention is not to degrade your office nor the SOAH. I have been intimated by the sheer volume
of legal requirements being asked of me and a compressed timeline that even the most experienced lawyers cannot
manage. Representing myself and my family in a hearing in Austin, listening to lawyers objecting one another, the
entering of motions, RFI's, testimony, exhibits, multiple web sites, and cross examinations of expert witnesses, and
neighbors pushing these lines on each other. All ofthis while I must continue to work to keep a small business from
failing and provide employee's a way to feed and clothe their families.

This proceeding concerns one of the largest transmission projects ever proposed in Texas. ALIs in other dockets have
stated this is the largest and most complex project the SOAH has ever seen. The Applicants with all their resources of
high-powered lawyers, hundreds of experts, and billions of dollars, seek authority to construct 765-kV transmission line
infrastructure across hundreds of miles of Texas, thousands of acres of private property, affecting thousands of
landowners like me, and imposing billions of dollars of costs upon Texas ratepayers. They are the ones to prove there is a
need. A real need based on accurate data and engineering principles. The only need the Applicants have proven is the
need to make billions of dollars off the backs of the ratepayers of Texas.

I am a proud member of a grassroots statewide coalition of private citizens, farmers, ranchers, country music artist, and
state representatives. We are committed to stand with fellow Texans where big government and powerful corporation
have overreached their authority. We are for progress. Build with us not over us! Now, as Paul Harvey says," Here is the
rest of the story"

The authority sought by Applicants is extraordinary. It includes the power of eminent domain, the ability to permanently
burden private property with transmission easements, and the ability to transfer substantial project costs to the citizens of
Texas. Because the authority requested is extraordinary, the burden imposed upon the Applicants is equally significant.



                                                              1
 The Applicants must prove compliance with PURA, Commission rules, all statutory requirements, and basic Texas and
U.S. constitutional rights afforded to private citizens. They must prove the project is needed. They must demonstrate that
the selected routes reasonably balance engineering requirements, landowner impacts, community values, prudent
avoidance, geographic diversity, and the public interest. Importantly, they must also demonstrate compliance with the
public participation and notification requirements established by the Commission.

The evidence presented demonstrates that the Applicants failed to satisfy those burdens.

The record establishes significant deficiencies concerning:

    •   Need for the project;
    •   Compliance with 2023 House Bill (HB) 5066 and the 2024 Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP);
    •   Failure to quantify actual power transfer requirements;
    •   Failure to quantify the amount of power Import Path 2 would deliver;
    •   Failure to provide proper notice under 16 TAC §22.52;
    •   Failure to provide meaningful public participation opportunities;
    •   Failure to utilize "current" county tax records;
    •   Failure to adequately identify and evaluate community values;
    •   Failure to implement meaningful prudent avoidance;
    •   Failure to adequately investigate schools, churches, and residences;
    •   Failure to provide meaningful geographic diversity with the top routes of interest that continuously impact the
        same families;
    •   Failure to accurately identify habitable structures;
    •   Failure to disclose the inclusion of travel trailers as habitable structures;
    •   Failure to exercise adequate quality assurance and quality control;
    •   Failure to demonstrate that Import Path 2 is needed by 2030.

For these reasons, the Administrative Law Judges (ALJ's) should recommend denial of the Application, and the
Commission should ultimately deny the requested Certificate of Convenience and Necessity.

II. SUMMARY OF GROUNDS FOR DENIAL

The evidence supports denial of the Application for the following independent reasons:

A. Failure to Demonstrate Need

Applicants are required to demonstrate the need as stated in their application for CCN;

No . 14 . "Need for the Proposed Project " to "describe the need for the construction and state how the proposed project
will address the need >' ( Reference Oncor & LCRA TSC Exhibit No . 1 , p . 19 )

The Applicants failed to establish a quantifiable and actionable need for the project as required by PURA. The
Application does not identify:

    •   The specific MW deficiency requiring correction;
    •   The specific MW import requirement at Big Hill;
    •   The specific MW import requirement at Sand Lake;
    •   The amount of power available at Bell County East;
    •   The amount of power expected to flow across Import Path 2;
    •   The amount of reliability improvement provided by Import Path 2.

Without identifying the actual need, Applicants cannot demonstrate that the proposed project appropriately addresses that
need.

                                                              2
 B. Failure to Demonstrate Import Path 2 Is Needed By 2030 and Misrepresentation of 2023 HB 5066

The two key planning documents to justify Import Path 2 is the 2024 PBRP and 2023 HB 5066 as referenced in the
application (References Exhibit JG-R-1, HB5066; Exhibit JG-2, PBRP).

The Applicant continues to misrepresent the application need by stating the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) or
2025 RTP justifies all three Import Paths are needed by 2030, but the application filed only relies on 2024 PBRP and 2023
HB 5066.

The 2024 PBRP indicates that Import Path 2 does not become necessary until approximately 2038.

ERCOT reaffirmed this conclusion in its December 12,2024, Sequencing Letter (Reference JKK Panel Ex 01)

The Applicant misrepresents the objectives of HB5066 in their application by stating the following:
1) extend transmission service to areas where mineral resources have been found;
2) increase available transmission capacity to meet forecasted load; and
3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without access to transmission service.

HB5066 not does state 2) increase available transmission capacity to meet forecasted load. Instead HB5066 states 2)
address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted loads. The Applicants addition of the word "transmission "
misrepresents the original objective of HB5066 and creates a monstrous project impacting thousands of private
landowners.

Twenty-five Texas Legislators have reaffirmed in a letter dated May 11,2026. The Applicants have misrepresented HB
5066 saying it mandates transmission as the only option to solve the electrification reliability ofthe Permian Basin
(Reference John Burrow Direct Testimony Page 23).

The application filed on March 26,2026, contains no persuasive evidence demonstrating that ERCOT's 2038 need
determination was ever formally reversed.

C. Failure to Comply with Notice Requirements

Applicants failed to provide meaningful notice and meaningful participation opportunities to approximately 1,400 affected
landowners.

Applicants added approximately 400 miles of new route links after public meetings had concluded in June 2025.

These additions dramatically expanded the number of affected properties from approximately 2,800 to approximately
4,200, a thirty-three percent increase.

The Applicant held critical information from the newly affected property owners for six months (Reference JB Exhibit 2)

Despite these substantial modifications, no additional public meetings were conducted as required by TAC 22.52 (4) (a).

D. Failure to Comply with TAC 22.52

Applicants failed to satisfy both the letter and intent of 16 TAC §22.52.

The rule exists to ensure affected landowners who are to receive an application receive direct notice and allowed
meaningful participation opportunities before route selection decisions become fixed.

Approximately one-third of affected landowners were denied those opportunities.


                                                              3
 E. Failure to Properly Evaluate Community Values

Applicants repeatedly testified that public participation meetings are critical for identifying community values. Yet
Applicants denied approximately 1,400 landowners any opportunity to participate in those meetings.

Applicants presented little evidence demonstrating that community values were:

    •   Tabulated;
    •   Ranked;
    •   Summarized;
    •   Compared;
    •   Incorporated into route selection.

F. Failure to Implement Prudent Avoidance

Applicants failed to demonstrate meaningful efforts to avoid or reduce impacts upon:

    •   Schools;
    •   Churches;
    •   Residences;
    •   Honiesteads;
    •   Community resources;
    •   Areas where people routinely gather.

The record contains numerous examples where Applicants either failed to identify and correctly categorized critical
habitable structures such as schools or churches and failed to demonstrate any meaningful effort to avoid them.

G. Failure to Exercise Due Diligence

Applicants failed to conduct adequate field verification and failed to exercise due diligence in identifying:

    •   Schools;
    •   Churches;
    •   Habitable structures;
    •   Future transportation infrastructure;
    •   Community resources;
    •   Geographic diversity concerns.

These deficiencies undermine confidence in the route location study and the resulting recommendations.

H. Failure to Utilize Current Tax Records

The evidence demonstrates Applicants did not consistently utilize current county appraisal district and tax roll information
when establishing ownership and mailing addresses.

As a result, as many as 27 affected landowners including Christine Thies and Shawn Hoffman were not notified until June
1,2026,67 days after the application was filed thus, they were deprived of notice opportunities required by Commission
rules. (Reference Exhibit JKK Panel 10 thru 13)




I. Failure to Maintain Adequate Quality Assurance and Quality Control
                                                              4
 The numerous errors identified throughout this proceeding indicate a lack of adequate QA/QC procedures.

Examples include:

    •   Incorrect ownership information;
    •   Missing ownership information;
    •   Incorrect habitable structure classifications;
    •   Failure to identify schools;
    •   Failure to identify churches;
    •   Inclusion of travel trailers as habitable structures;
    •   Route evaluation deficiencies;
    •   Notification deficiencies.

The cumulative effect of these errors undermines confidence in the Application and supporting studies.

III. APPLICANTS FAILED TO PROVE NEED FOR THE PROJECT PURA §37.056(c)

The burden of proving need rests entirely upon the Applicants.

Landowners are not required to prove the project is unnecessary.

Rather, Applicants must affirmatively demonstrate both: 1) a quantifiable need; and 2) that the proposed project addresses
that need.

Applicants failed to satisfy either requirement.

A. The Application Relies Entirely Upon 2023 HB 5066 and the 2024 PBRP

Applicants' need case relies almost exclusively upon:

    •   2023 HB 5066; and
    •   ERCOT's 2024 PBRP.

Neither document independently establishes the need for this specific project.

HB 5066 authorized development of a plan to address reliability concerns in the Permian Basin.

HB 5066 did not mandate construction of Import Path 2.

HB 5066 did not mandate construction of a Bell County East to Big Hill transmission line.

HB 5066 did not require transmission-only solutions.

Instead, HB 5066 required consideration of methods such as generation alternatives to address increasing capacity needs.

These facts are substantiated by the previously mentioned Texas State Legislators letter, dated May 11, 2026.

ERCOT's 2024 RBPB states Import Paths 2 need starts to appear in 2038, a need twelve years in the future.




B. Applicants Failed to Quantify Actual Need


                                                                5
 Applicants never identify:

    •   The specific MW deficit at Big Hill;
    •   The specific MW deficit at Sand Lake;
    •   The amount of import power required;
    •   The amount of import power available;
    •   The amount of power expected to flow on Import Path 2.

The Application repeatedly references future load growth but never translates those forecasts into a specific, actionable
need capable of supporting construction of this project.

The Commission cannot determine whether the proposed solution is appropriately sized when the underlying need has
never been quantified.

The Applicants only response when questioned is HB 5066 mandates the use of transmission (a misrepresentation) and
ERCOT came up with the numbers when in fact the transmission providers provide those numbers.

C. Applicants Failed to Demonstrate the Project's Ability to Address Any Quantified Need

The Application also fails to explain:

    •   How much power would flow through Import Path 2;
    •   When that power would flow;
    •   Where that power originates;
    •   Whether Bell County East has sufficient available generation;
    •   Whether transmission constraints elsewhere would limit delivery.

Without these fundamental facts, the Commission cannot determine whether the proposed project would solve the
problem Applicants claim exists.

D. Applicants' Bi-Directional Flow Assertions Are Unsupported

Applicants assert the project will improve bi-directional power flow.

However:

    •   HB 5066 does not identify bi-directional flow as a project objective;
    •   The 2024 PBRP does not identify bi-directional flow as a project objective;
    •   The project is title as "Import Path" from East Bell County to Big Hill;
    •   The Application contains no engineering analysis validating this claim.

The reference appears unsupported and cannot substitute for proof of need.

E. Recent Evidence Undermines the Load Forecasts Supporting the Project

Evidence presented during the hearing demonstrates that significant reductions have occurred in projected load growth
assumptions relied upon by ERCOT.

The Commission should carefully evaluate whether the forecasts supporting Import Path 2 remain valid.

Ifthe underlying forecasts are materially overstated, then the need determination supporting the project is similarly
undermined.


                                                             6
 IV. IMPORT PATH 2 IS NOT NEEDED UNTIL APPROXIMATELY 2038

The strongest evidence regarding timing comes directly from ERCOT.

ERCOT's 2024 Permian Basin Reliability Plan indicates that Import Path 2 need does not start to appear until 2038.

ERCOT subsequently reinforced that conclusion through its December 12,2024, Sequencing Letter.

In that letter, ERCOT Vice President Ms. Kristi Hobbs stated that projects needed to serve forecasted 2030 load should be
prioritized ahead of projects needed to serve forecasted 2038 load.

ERCOT's Ms. Kristi Hobbs further advised that only two of the three proposed 765-kV import paths were needed by
2030.

Import Path 2 was not identified as one ofthose priority projects.

Ms. Hobbs appeared before the Commission during the December 19,2024, open meeting and was available to answer
questions concerning the Sequencing Letter. The Commission open meeting public record contains no evidence that
ERCOT formally withdrew or changed the Sequencing Letter.

The 2024 RTP was released on Dec 20,2026, one day after the Commission's open meeting on December 19,2024. The
Applicants claim appears to be that ERCOT changed their load findings in one day on a very large critical study that takes
months to develop resulting in negative impacts to thousands of acres of Texas farms and ranches and thousands of
hardworking Texans. This does not add up.

Consequently, the most credible planning evidence before the Commission demonstrates that Import Path 2 is not required
in 2030 and that HB5066 does not mandate import path 2.

Given the impacts to landowners associated with this project, the Commission should not authorize eminent domain and
burden billions of dollars of infrastructure costs on Texas ratepayers based upon a speculative future requirement that
ERCOT determined does not materialize for twelve years.

V. FAILURE TO PROVIDE REQUIRED PUBLIC NOTICE AND MEANINGFUL PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
PURA §37.054, PURA §37.056, and 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4)

The Commission's routing process depends upon meaningful public participation. Public participation cannot occur when
affected landowners are not informed that a project exists.

The evidence demonstrates and Applicants admit by their on testimony they expanded the project after the June 2025
public meetings yet failed to provide the 1,400 newly affected landowners the same participation opportunities afforded to
earlier landowners.

This failure undermined the integrity ofthe routing process and deprived approximately 1,400 landowners of the
opportunity to provide information concerning community values, routing constraints, prudent avoidance considerations,
and alternative route locations.




A. Public Meetings Were Conducted Before the Project Was Fully Defined



                                                             7
 Applicants conducted public meetings during June 2025. At that time, approximately 2,800 property owners were
identified as affected landowners that would receive notice of application were invited to participate.

Applicants repeatedly testified throughout this proceeding that public meetings serve a critical function in route
development and route refinement.

Applicants represented that public meetings were intended to:

    •   Gather community value information;
    •   Identify routing constraints;
    •   Obtain local knowledge;
    •   Identify residences and sensitive receptors;
    •   Identify schools and churches;
    •   Evaluate route alternatives;
    •   Improve route selection.

The Commission's rules recognize the importance of these public meetings and require them because public participation
is a necessary component ofthe routing process.

However, the project presented in the March 26,2026, Application was materially different from the project presented
during the June 2025 public meetings. Over 400 miles ofnew alternative routes were added.

B. Applicants Expanded the Project Scope After Public Meetings

The evidence demonstrates that after completion ofthe June 2025 public meetings, Applicants:

    •   Removed approximately 140 miles of route links;
    •   Modified approximately 68 miles of route links;
    •   Added approximately 400 miles of entirely new route links;
    •   Increased affected properties from approximately 2,800 to approximately 4,200.

These changes are not minor adjustments; they fundamentally altered the project and greatly expanded the number of
affected landowners.

The addition of approximately 400 miles of route links represents one of the most significant route modifications in any
transmission routing proceeding.

Yet despite these substantial changes, Applicants conducted no additional public meetings, did not notify PUC staff, only
stating they exceeded what was required by code (Reference JB Exhibit 2).

C. Approximately 1,400 Landowners Were Never Afforded the Opportunity to Attend a Public Meeting

The evidence demonstrates that approximately 1,400 ultimately affected property owners never received notice of a public
meeting.

These landowners never had the opportunity to:

    •   Meet with project representatives;
    •   Ask questions;
    •   Review route alternatives;
    •   Identify routing constraints;
    •   Provide local knowledge;
    •   Identify community values;
    •   Suggest alternative routes;
                                                              8
     •   Retain legal counsel during the preliminary stages ofthe project;

As a result, approximately one-third of all affected landowners were denied opportunities afforded to every landowner
notified during the June 2025 public meetings.

The Commission cannot reasonably conclude that public participation requirements were satisfied when one-third of
affected landowners never had the opportunity to participate.

D. Applicants Knew of These Additional Landowners Long Before Filing the Application

The evidence indicates Applicants had knowledge ofthe 400 miles of newly developed alternative route links six months
before filing the Application.

Despite this knowledge, Applicants:

    •   Did not notify the newly 1,400 affected landowners;
    •   Did not conduct additional public meetings;
    •   Did not provide meaningful outreach;
    •   Did not provide equal participation opportunities
    •   Did not inform the PUC staff.

Applicants cannot simultaneously argue that that they exceeded what was required and that public participation is critical
while withholding participation opportunities from approximately 1,400 affected landowners.

Both positions cannot be true.

If public participation is important enough to require public meetings, then all affected landowners must be given a
meaningful opportunity to participate.

E. Late Notice Further Prejudiced Newly Affected Landowners

The prejudice suffered by newly affected landowners continued after filing of the Application. Twenty-seven or more
landowners may not have been notified weeks to months after the application was filed

The record contains evidence that certain landowners, including Christine Thies and Shane Hoffman, did not receive
notification ofthe Application until June 1,2026 (Reference JKK Panel 10 thru 13).

This occurred approximately 67 days after the March 26,2026, filing of the Application.

By that time:

    •   Procedural deadlines were already approaching;
    •   Discovery schedules were underway;
    •   Expert witnesses had been retained by other parties;
    •   Significant strategic decisions had already occurred.

These landowners entered the proceeding months behind parties who had received earlier notice.




F. Lack of Notice Severely Limited Access to Counsel

                                                                9
 The consequences of delayed notice extended beyond procedural deadlines.

 1,400 Landowners were not afforded an opportunity of a public meeting, they became aware ofthis project only after
receiving the notice ofthe application after March 26,2026, faced substantial difficulty or was not able to obtain qualified
legal representation.

All attorneys with specialized knowledge of transmission line litigation like Mr. Bayliff and Mr. Brady, had already been
retained by other parties and the parties who had been notified months earlier.

Landowners who received notice months later entered the process at a significant disadvantage through no fault of their
own.


This disparity is precisely why meaningful notice is required before an application

VI. APPLICANTS FAILED TO COMPLY WITH THE INTENT OF 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4)

Applicants have repeatedly argued that compliance with 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) was satisfied because public meetings were
conducted in June 2025. This argument ignores the broader purpose and intent ofthe rule.

Applicant direct testimony from Ms. Casey D. Petty indicates either a misunderstanding or another misrepresentation of
code.
In her direct testimony, Ms. Petty was asked "DID THE APPLICANTS HOLD A PUBLIC PARTICIPATION MEETING
BEFORE FILING THE APPLICATION? "

Ms. Petty's answer was "Yes. As discussed in Sections 2.5 and 5.0 ofthe Environmental Assessment and Routing Study,
the Applicants hosted three public open-house meetings for the proposed transmission line project. Because at least 25
landowners were entitled to receive notice based on the preliminary alternative routes. a public meeting was required
under 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4)"

Ms. Petty's answer makes one to believe that only landowners on preliminary alternative routes that were entitled to
receive direct mail notice of the application are afforded the opportunity to participate in a public meeting. This is furthest
from the truth.

The code makes no distinction between the 2,800 landowners on preliminary alternative routes invited to the public
meeting and the 1,400 landowners on the newly added alternative routes not invited to the public meeting regardless of
the date a route is added.

16 TAC §11.51(«4) is dear, "The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the filing if 25 or more persons
would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application.

Both the 1,400 and 2,800 landowners are entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application and thus both, by code,
are afforded the opportunity to participate in a public meeting. The Applicant chose not to abide.

16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) states "The utility must hold at least one public meeting. This wording supports the situation we
are now in. It provides the flexibility to hold additional public meetings to support the addition of new alternative routes
with landowners numbering more than 25. Ifthis was not the case, the code would simply state "must hold one public
meeting"

The ALI s and Commission must not view this as a check the box rule and require the Applicant to adhere to this
important and critical rule.

The Commission and the codes exist to ensure affected Texans have a meaningful opportunity to participate before
routing decisions are finalized.
                                                              10
 A. The Purpose of The Rule Is Public Participation

The scope ofthe project expanded to include 1,400 new affected landowners.

16 TAC § 22 . 52 ( a)( 4 ) purpose is clear, " The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the filing if 25 or more
persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application."

The rule is not to create disparity among landowners but rather to create meaningful opportunity to participate for all
landowners.

The new 1,400 landowners on the added 400 miles of new alternative routes would be entitled to receive direct mail
notice of the application and thus should have been afforded the opportunity to participate in one public meeting.

The rule recognizes that meaningful public participation is essential when routing major transmission projects.

Public meetings are not a box to be checked. Public meetings are the mechanism through which landowners provide:

    •    Community value information;
    •    Routing constraints;
    •    School locations;
    •    Church locations;
    •    Future development plans;
    •    Local knowledge.

When approximately 1,400 landowners never receive that opportunity, the purpose of the rule has not been achieved.

B. Applicants' Interpretation Produces an Absurd Result

Under Applicants' interpretation:

    1.   Public meetings could be conducted for one set of landowners but not others;
    2.   Hundreds of miles of new route links could later be added;
    3.   Thousands of additional acres could become affected;
    4.   More than 1,400 new landowners could become impacted;
    5.   No additional public outreach would ever be required.

This interpretation defeats the purpose of the rule and eliminates meaningful public participation for newly affected
landowners.

The ALI s and Commission should reject that interpretation.

C. The Record Demonstrates Actual Harm

The record demonstrates actual harm.

Approximately 1,400 landowners:

    •    Lost the opportunity to attend public meetings;
    •    Lost the opportunity to provide routing information;
    •    Lost the opportunity to identify community values;
    •    Lost the opportunity to influence route development;
    •    Lost months of preparation time;
    •    Lost access to available legal resources.

                                                                 11
 These harms are real, measurable, and directly attributable to Applicants' failure to provide equivalent participation
opportunities.

D. Relief for the 1,400 Landowners Is Appropriate

The Commission has the authority to ensure fairness and protect the public interest. Landowners who were denied
participation opportunities should receive equivalent relief.

The evidence supports a finding that newly affected landowners lost approximately 206 days of participation opportunity
compared to those invited to the June 2025 public meetings.

VII. DUE PROCESS CONCERNS

The United States Constitution and Texas Constitution guarantee fundamental due process protections.

Among those protections are:

    •   Notice;
    •   Opportunity to be heard;
    •   Meaningful participation;
    •   Opportunity to present evidence;
    •   Opportunity to challenge evidence.

Those protections become especially important when governmental action may ultimately result in the taking of private
property through eminent domain.

When affected landowners are not provided timely notice and meaningful participation opportunities, due process
concerns necessarily arise.

The Commission should not authorize a project of this magnitude where substantial numbers of affected Texans were
denied the same participation opportunities afforded to others.

VIII. COMMUNITY VALUES PURA §37.056(c)(4)(A)

Community values are one of the express routing factors the Commission is required to consider when determining
whether a proposed transmission line route is in the public interest.

Applicants repeatedly testified that public participation meetings were an essential component of identifying community
values and obtaining local information necessary for route selection.

Applicants' own Environmental Assessment and Route Location Study state that public outreach was intended to Identify
community values; Identify local concerns; Identify routing constraints; Gather local knowledge; Improve route selection.

Despite repeatedly emphasizing the importance of public participation, Applicants denied approximately 1,400 affected
landowners the opportunity to participate in those meetings.

As a result, a substantial portion of the community value information that should have been considered was never
collected.

The Commission cannot reasonably conclude that community values were adequately identified and considered when
approximately one-third of affected landowners never had an opportunity to provide them.

A. Applicants Failed to Demonstrate Community Values Were Actually Used

                                                             12
 While Applicants repeatedly referenced community values throughout this proceeding, the record contains little evidence
demonstrating how community value information was incorporated into route selection.

The evidence demonstrates that community value information may have been collected from some landowners, but
Applicants failed to show how that information was systematically evaluated and incorporated into the route development
process.
The Commission should give little weight to generalized statements that community values were considered when the
record contains no meaningful demonstration of how they were evaluated.

B. Community Values Cannot Be Fully Evaluated When One-Third of Affected Landowners Are Excluded

Applicants' route development process excluded approximately 1,400 affected landowners from public participation
opportunities.

Those landowners were denied the ability to provide information regarding:

    •      Existing residences;
    •      Family-owned ranches;
    •      Agricultural operations;
    •      Schools;
    •      Churches;
    •      Community gathering areas;
    •      Planned developments;
    •      Recreational uses;
    •      Conservation efforts.

Because this information was never collected from a substantial portion of affected landowners, the resulting community
value analysis is necessarily incomplete.

IX. GEOGRAPHIC DIVERSITY PURA §37.056(c)(4)

The Commission has long recognized that geographic diversity is an important routing consideration because it prevents
the repeated concentration of transmission impacts on the same families, properties, communities, and public resources.

The evidence demonstrates that Applicants failed to meaningfully apply geographic diversity principles to Route Links
G71, G72, and G73.

Instead of spreading impacts across the broader study area, Applicants repeatedly concentrated impacts on the same
landowners, the same residences, the same agricultural operations, and the same community resources.

A. New Alternate Route Links G71, G72, And G73 Repeatedly Impact the Same Families

The evidence demonstrates that new alternative Route Links G71, G72, and G73 repeatedly affect the same properties and
families throughout the route development process.

Rather than creating meaningful route separation and geographic diversity, these route links repeatedly converge upon the
same affected landowners.

The same residences are repeatedly impacted; the same agricultural operations are repeatedly impacted; the same
community resources are repeatedly impacted; the same property owners bear a disproportionate share of project burdens.
This is the opposite of geographic diversity.

These same landowners are among the 1,400 landowners that were not invited to a public meeting.
                                                           13
 If they were afforded this opportunity, they would have provided comment on geographic diversity concerns.

The Commission should recognize this unfairness could have been resolved ifthese landowners had the opportunity to
participate.

B. Route Links G71, G72 And G73 Dominate the Applicants' Preferred Routes

The record demonstrates that Route Links G71, G72 and G73 are heavily represented throughout Applicants' route
analysis.

Specifically:

    •   G72 and G73 are included within Route 894, the Applicants' Best Meets Route;
    •   G72 and G73 are included within Route 487, PUC Staff Recommendation;
    •   G71 and G73 are included within Route 392, Top Eight Routes of Interest
    •   G72 and G73 appear in all six of Applicants' Top Six Routes;
    •   G72 and G73 appear in twenty-seven of Applicants' Top Thirty Routes;
    •   G72 and G73 appear in ninety-two of the one hundred twenty-two routes identified in the Application.

These statistics demonstrate that the Applicants repeatedly relied upon the same route links while simultaneously claiming

XVI. CONSTITUTIONAL AND DUE PROCESS CONCERNS

The authority sought by Applicants ultimately depends upon the power of eminent domain. Accordingly, constitutional
protections become particularly important.

The Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I of the Texas Constitution protect citizens from
deprivation of property without due process of law.

Those protections require, at a minimum:

    •   Meaningful notice;
    •   Meaningful opportunity to be heard;
    •   Meaningful opportunity to participate;
    •   Fundamental fairness.

A. Due Process Requires Meaningful Notice

Notice is not a technical requirement. Notice is the foundation upon which all other procedural rights depend.

A landowner who does not know a project exists cannot:

    •   Attend public meetings;
    •   Provide routing information;
    •   Obtain legal counsel;
    •   Participate in route development;
    •   Protect property rights.

The evidence demonstrates that approximately 1,400 landowners were denied these opportunities.

B. Due Process Requires Meaningful Opportunity to Participate

Meaningful participation requires more than receiving notice after critical decisions have already occurred.

                                                            21
 The evidence demonstrates that many landowners entered this proceeding months after public meetings had concluded
and months after route development decisions had been made.

Such participation is inherently unequal.

C. Due Process Concerns Are Heightened in Eminent Domain Proceedings

The Commission is not merely selecting a route. The Commission is deciding whether private property may ultimately be
condemned for the benefit ofthis project.

Because eminent domain authority may follow from the Commission's decision, strict adherence to notice and
participation requirements is essential.
